final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines it should not matter much which office goes first, and splitting the case into two prosecutions gains nothing. The best course is a single prosecution by whichever office can bring all of the charged executions of the scheme with proper venue. If the two offices cannot consolidate, the first office to indict and sentence should be the one holding the larger share of the fraudulent claims and loss. My conclusion on that last point is a reasoned inference, not a rule I found stated in an authority.

1. Relevant conduct reaches across districts. Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), a fraud sentence is based on all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan, including conduct in another state or district and uncharged conduct. A court sentencing on the South Carolina counts would count the Georgia loss, and the reverse. Either office therefore gets the full aggregate loss under 2B1.1(b)(1). The health-care-fraud enhancement for government health care program losses over $1 million, 2B1.1(b)(7), would also be driven by the combined amount. I did not verify the 2B1.1(b)(7) text in this run.

2. Grouping. If both sets of counts were in one case, 3D1.2(d) groups fraud counts, and the offense level is set by the total loss. A single combined case does not multiply the guideline range. Stacking is available only through 5G1.2(d), and only if the range exceeds the statutory maximum of any one count. Section 1347 carries a 10-year maximum per count, or 20 years if serious bodily injury results, or life if death results. Many counts could therefore permit consecutive sentences when the guideline range is high.

3. Sequential prosecutions do not add time. If the first district sentences the doctor and takes the other state's conduct as relevant conduct, then 5G1.3(b) requires the second district's sentence to run concurrently with the remainder of the undischarged term, with an adjustment for time already served. The Commission's own materials describe this as applying where a defendant is prosecuted in two or more federal jurisdictions for the same course of conduct. Prosecuting in two districts therefore does not add prison time, and it risks the second court granting credit or a downward variance.

4. Venue limits the single-indictment option. Venue lies for each count where the offense was committed, and 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) allows venue in any district where a continuing offense was begun, continued or completed. Each execution of a scheme under 1347 is arguably a separate offense. If so, the Georgia claims could not be charged in South Carolina, and the reverse. I did not research the case law on venue for a multi-district 1347 scheme, so this point is unresolved. If venue exists for the full scheme in only one district, that office should indict.

5. Circuit law is no longer a meaningful differentiator. South Carolina is in the Fourth Circuit and Southern Georgia is in the Eleventh. The circuits differed on whether Application Note 3(A) of 2B1.1 (intended loss) deserved deference after Kisor, and the Eleventh Circuit en banc in United States v. Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269 (2023), is my recollection of the main case. I did not verify that citation in this run. The Commission resolved the split by moving the loss definitions into the guideline text, effective November 1, 2024 (Amendment 827). Sentencing today uses the same loss rule in both districts, so circuit differences should not favor either office. Other circuit-specific differences, for example on health care fraud loss presumptions, were not researched.

6. Practical recommendation. To maximize time, consolidate: one indictment, with all counts for which venue exists, so that 3D1.2(d) grouping and 5G1.2 stacking are available. Failing consolidation, the office with the larger loss and claim volume should indict and sentence first. Its court then captures the full relevant conduct, and the other office's case adds nothing. Because the two offices are otherwise symmetrical on the facts given, I cannot name one office over the other.

authorities.title: Imposition of a Sentence on a Defendant Subject to an Undischarged Term of Imprisonment
authorities.proposition: Where the undischarged term resulted from conduct that is relevant conduct to the instant offense, the new sentence runs concurrently with the remainder and is adjusted for time served. The Commission's materials say this applies to prosecutions in two or more federal jurisdictions.

authorities.title: Relevant Conduct
authorities.proposition: Acts that are part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan count in the guideline calculation, including uncharged conduct.

authorities.title: Loss definitions moved from commentary to guideline text
authorities.proposition: The Commission moved the actual and intended loss definitions into the 2B1.1 text, resolving the circuit split over Application Note 3(A).

authorities.title: Health care fraud
authorities.proposition: Ten-year maximum per count, 20 years if serious bodily injury results, and life if death results.

authorities.title: Offenses begun in one district and completed in another
authorities.proposition: Continuing offenses may be prosecuted in any district where they were begun, continued or completed.

claims.text: Other-state fraud conduct is relevant conduct, so either office reaches the full loss.
A second sentence on relevant conduct must run concurrently under 5G1.3(b), so two prosecutions add no prison time.
Since November 2024, 2B1.1 loss rules are uniform across circuits, removing a circuit-based reason to prefer one office.
Statutory maximums per count and venue limits shape how many consecutive years a combined case can reach.
